cards.heading: Definition
cards.question: What is request-level sandbox isolation?
cards.answer: Deploying only the changed services as an ephemeral overlay on a shared baseline Kubernetes cluster, then routing individual requests into that overlay via a header-borne routing key propagated on every downstream call.

cards.heading: Two required halves
cards.question: What two mechanisms must both hold for request-level sandbox isolation to work?
cards.answer: Request routing (mesh or sidecar deciding baseline vs. sandbox at each hop) and application-layer context propagation (carrying the routing key header across every hop) — either alone is insufficient.

cards.heading: How routing is enforced
cards.question: How is request routing to the sandbox enforced at each hop?
cards.answer: By configuring a service mesh such as Istio to route on the header, or by attaching a dedicated lightweight sidecar proxy to each workload when no mesh is present.

cards.heading: How propagation works
cards.question: How does the routing key survive every hop between services?
cards.answer: Via an OpenTelemetry-based library that copies the header from each incoming request onto every outgoing request — automatic in some languages, manual in others.

cards.heading: Failure mode
cards.question: What happens when a service fails to propagate the routing header?
cards.answer: It silently falls back to the baseline service rather than failing loudly — this is the mechanism's main failure mode.

cards.heading: vs. remocal development
cards.question: How does request-level sandbox isolation differ from remocal development in what it isolates?
cards.answer: Remocal development binds a local process to one remote pod's traffic; request-level sandbox isolation runs changed services in-cluster and routes tagged requests to them, letting many sandboxes coexist on the same shared cluster.
